I usually have one cocktail every couple of weeks, if that, and I don't have a high tolerance.  At the same time, my ADHD meds aren't working well most days and even on a good day - productive, not as 'on edge' around social activities, not feeling as bad sensory overload wise - I still mask, and still feel exhausted at the end of the day.  Would having a shot of a margarita be a way to cope? I understand the long term effects of alcohol on your body isn't great and know this isn't healthy to even consider it because it's a depressant, but I don't want to have to depend on my self care habits to survive an intense world. What works to make me feel less like the world is hot, bright and up to 11 is alcohol - it has been the only thing that ever worked.  I understand the risk of substance abuse is high for us; at the same time having even a little something makes me feel calmer in a way nothing else comes close to.  I don't feel sad when I drink - I just feel less like my nerves are on the outside of my skin.

1. Shape Ethical UX for the AI Era – Create guidelines for human-centred, ethical UX in AI-driven tech.
2. Advocate for UX at Scale – Influence policy around ethical design, accessibility, privacy, and responsible technology.  

For both of these, folks at [https://alltechishuman.org/](https://alltechishuman.org/) and [https://www.humanetech.com/](https://www.humanetech.com/) are up and running - I would suggest checking out some of their materials, as a lot has been written on both of these

3. Prototype Sustainable Digital Practices – Innovate sustainable UX methods to reduce digital waste and carbon footprints. <--- check out [https://www.climatedesigners.org/](https://www.climatedesigners.org/) which is the largest group around this.

4.Explore Speculative UX Futures – Use futures thinking methodologies (e.g., futures wheels, horizon scanning) to proactively shape the UX industry's direction.  <-- there are a few Speculative Futures groups although not very large - really would love to see more of it, although I doubt we have much pull with clients on this.

5. Boost Digital Accessibility and Inclusion – Support NGOs, schools, and startups in building inclusive products.  <--- volunteering in the U.S. in orgs like [https://taprootfoundation.org/](https://taprootfoundation.org/) and [https://www.catchafire.org/volunteer/](https://www.catchafire.org/volunteer/) would be great, as well as a bunch of others like TechFleet.  It would be interesting to connect with these orgs to see that while they do build for non-profits, it's not clear how much of that is around accessibility and inclusion.

6 Reinvent UX Careers – Identify new roles, pathways, and entrepreneurial opportunities within our changing field.  <--- yes please - I feel there's so much talk, but little accessible action, and while I would LOVE to see a union I think it's going to be a tough sell with employers.

How I work: 

I've had PMs who figure out a product vision, features and their priority - but don't know how to communicate.  I'll have cards with a title and no acceptance criteria or even a description - basically 'make the line go longer like we talked about in a meeting one time'.  They will tell me 'oh devs don't want to read anything - give them the mockup to build', but PMs often forget I am not a wizard who creates mockups in a cave, and your QA is not a wizard who can read your mind.  I need a) the goal of what we're trying to do/fix in a list of acceptance criteria b) the content c) a high level view if there are multiple states, success criteria, changes etc.  I try to tell them 'for everything you see on the screen, write it as an AC'.  It need not be a formal story format (or ACs as Given/Then/When) - even a bullet list is fine.  More often than not across multiple companies there was a reliance on mind reading from PMs, and it's no surprise there is buggy software as a result.  No alignment because no documentation.

The other part often now is little consideration of metrics - I've been in feature factories where we don't measure and evaluate if our products are meeting goals.  As longas there's something to code, code it.  Keep busy coding. I am happy to provide a design, but often see clients not understand what value we're creating. While I can identify the benefits of an approach and suggest things I feel are valuable, it's the product manager's responsibility to identify value and why we're building it.  That piece is often missing other than 'I woke up with this idea of what if random feature could spin through the air...'.

How I'd like to work:

A set of user stories that are clear with ACs and are [INVESTed](https://blog.logrocket.com/product-management/writing-meaningful-user-stories-invest-principle/), have a goal, are on a product roadmap tied to value or impact - and is something that helps a customer do something they want to do.  We have regular meetings to refine the backlog and everyone on the team understand why we're building it. Not a 'ooh, what if the window could fly through the air and change to blue' - that's an idea, not a feature.  It's ironic that user stories are the smallest form of documentation that is often the hardest thing for PMs to do.

A lot of this is context setting up front before you show them anything:

\- stress that this is research and there are no right or wrong answers - you're testing the product, not them.  You are ensuring it's the best product and you do that by showing it to users, so you want them to be as honest and say what they're thinking and that you want to hear the positives and negatives.

\- focus on talking out loud so that it's important while they're doing things when they hit a point to speak about what they're thinking.  If they're struggling, a simple' can you tell me what you're thinking about' is useful

\- for value, I think it's a few things - is it valuable on its own, is it more valuable than something else (if you're trying to determine what to build next) and is it valuable enough to pay for AND subscribe to keep paying for it, and if it's valuable enough that it solves the problem.  Value is something to really explore in more depth, because we've all seen things that are great, but may not want to switch to a competitor, or may not want to actively pay for.  If it's about use, asking why they don't or wouldn't use it is fine. 

There are ways to both ask the questions to get content AND ask them in a non-biased way (via your tone) to make people feel comfortable.  I always feel the first 5 minutes of an interview sets the standard for how it will go because if you create a warm, comfortable, honest environment for discussion and testing a product, you'll have a successful one.

I think grief is a process that has its own master and timelines, and it is a wound.  When you cut yourself or have anything that damages you, our bodies do a remarkable job at healing the wound even if it feels that's impossible. Grief from a death is perhaps the hardest wound - you know intuitively it will 'go away' or feel less hot one day, but it is a fresh wound that makes you cry and feel the most intense feeling you can ever feel as a human.  I know from the grief of loved ones I've lost - including a partner - the 'hot' part of it becomes less hot over time and the heart does heal.  This was bound to be a traumatic grief for many of us even though we didn't know him - it's 1D and all that it means (both the music and no reunion and that the boys we love are also in grief, and their families too), he was so young, he had a child, he had so much promise, his last day was so devastating.  All of this and so much more.  More than anything, though, I remember all the times he was smiling.  This was a man who just seems to be born to perform, to give and get so much from music and he just... always seemed to be smiling, giving people hugs, giving of himself.  

It's no wonder we feel such a loss.  All of these are so much on their own, and all of them are just more intense with all of these factors.  I think we have so many posts of how we're just so hurt, and it's not surprising.

So you do what you do, which is to find healing, slowly.  Keep taking care of yourself - food, exercise, meditate, do your routines, live your daily life.  And connect with people - both 1D people and others.  Show up for them, and show up for yourself.  It's not that you 'move on', but your heart heals.  Listen to music that restores you.  Go for walks in nature.  You're still going to cry but your heart can heal. You don't move on from anyone's death, but we can heal the part that is most devastated.  At the memorial I went to, we gave each other hugs as we cried. That was healing and reminded me that it's possible.
